quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Psychologists have discovered that many classic findings fail when other laboratories repeat the experiments. Part of the reason lies in incentives, because journals prefer novel, striking results and careers depend on publication. Researchers may therefore run several analyses and report only those that work. Some journals now accept studies before the results are known, judging them on the quality of the design. Early evidence suggests that these registered studies report far fewer positive findings, which is what one would expect if earlier reports were inflated. Yet critics point out that careful replication can also fail because of hidden differences in participants or procedures. The lesson many researchers draw is that a single study should never be treated as settled. Confidence should grow only as independent teams reach similar conclusions.
options: Publication incentives inflate results, so confidence should rest on repeated, independent findings rather than single studies.
Failed replications prove that classic psychological findings were invented, so registered studies are unnecessary.
Critics argue that replication failures reflect poor experiments, so single studies deserve confidence.
Registered studies report more positive findings than earlier research, which shows that design quality is irrelevant.
quests.correctAnswer: Publication incentives inflate results, so confidence should rest on repeated, independent findings rather than single studies.
quests.hint: Decide what the paragraph wants readers to do differently after finishing it.
quests.explanation: The paragraph traces unreliable results to incentives, describes a reform, admits complications and ends with a lesson about confidence. The wrong options overstate fraud, reverse the registered-study finding and misstate the critics.
keyPoints: Many classic psychology findings fail to replicate.
Incentives to publish striking results encourage selective reporting, and registered studies reduce it.
Replication itself can fail, so confidence should come from independent agreement.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Neighbourhoods with fewer trees can be several degrees hotter than leafy ones during a heatwave. Those neighbourhoods are often poorer, because trees were historically planted where property values were high. Residents of hotter districts suffer more heat-related illness, and they are less able to afford air conditioning. Cities are now planting trees in the hottest districts first. However, young trees need years to provide shade, and they need watering that cash-strapped councils may struggle to supply. Some residents worry that greening will raise rents and eventually push out the very people it was meant to help. Planners therefore combine planting with rent protection and community ownership of new parks. The heat problem, they say, cannot be separated from the housing problem.
options: Wealthier neighbourhoods suffer more heat illness because they contain fewer old trees than poorer ones.
Young trees provide shade quickly, so councils need not worry about watering or long delays.
Planting trees in hot districts lowers rents, so greening benefits poorer residents at once.
Urban heat is unequally distributed, so tree planting must be paired with protection against rising housing costs.
quests.correctAnswer: Urban heat is unequally distributed, so tree planting must be paired with protection against rising housing costs.
quests.hint: Test whether an option treats heat and housing as separate problems or as connected ones.
quests.explanation: The paragraph links heat exposure to income, notes practical limits on planting and warns that improvement can raise rents, so planners join the issues. The wrong options reverse the effect on rents, who suffers and how quickly shade appears.
keyPoints: Poorer neighbourhoods tend to have fewer trees and suffer more from heat.
Planting is slow and needs care, and greening can raise rents.
Planners pair trees with rent protection and community ownership.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Many central banks are independent of elected governments, so that interest rates are not set to win elections. Evidence suggests that independent banks tend to keep inflation lower. Yet critics say that decisions about jobs and prices are too important to leave to unelected officials. When banks buy government bonds on a large scale, they also affect who gains from rising asset prices. Defenders answer that the banks have clear targets set by law and must explain their decisions. Some observers propose that governments should set goals more explicitly and review them regularly. Others fear that any closer supervision would invite the very political pressure that independence prevents. The dispute is over how to keep accountability without giving up credibility.
options: Central banks are elected by voters, so their decisions on rates are democratic.
Central bank independence supports stable prices and keeping it accountable without political pressure is the challenge.
Defenders say the banks need little explanation of their decisions because the law fixes their targets.
Independent banks tend to raise inflation, which is why critics want governments to set rates.
quests.correctAnswer: Central bank independence supports stable prices and keeping it accountable without political pressure is the challenge.
quests.hint: Look for the tension between two goods that the final sentence names.
quests.explanation: Independence brings credibility, but it raises legitimacy questions that proposals for supervision may worsen, so the trade-off is accountability against credibility. The wrong options reverse how banks are chosen, the inflation record and the defenders' claim.
keyPoints: Independent central banks tend to keep inflation lower.
Critics question unelected control of jobs and prices and note effects on asset prices.
The debate is about combining accountability with credibility.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Regulators must decide how quickly to approve new medicines. Faster approval brings treatments to patients who may have no alternative, especially in rare or fatal illnesses. But shorter trials may miss rare side effects, which appear only when thousands of people take the drug. Some agencies grant conditional approval, requiring companies to continue gathering data after launch. Follow-up studies are not always completed, and drugs remain on the market even when the evidence remains weak. Patient groups argue that people facing death should be allowed to take some risk. Safety advocates reply that patients cannot make informed choices without reliable evidence. Every system therefore reflects a judgement about how much uncertainty society will tolerate.
options: Patient groups argue that people facing death should wait for complete evidence before taking a drug.
Conditional approval guarantees that follow-up studies are completed after a drug enters the market.
Faster approval eliminates the risk of rare side effects because trials are shortened and simplified.
Drug approval speed trades early access against reliable evidence, reflecting a judgement about tolerable uncertainty.
quests.correctAnswer: Drug approval speed trades early access against reliable evidence, reflecting a judgement about tolerable uncertainty.
quests.hint: Try summarising in your own words what every regulatory system has to decide.
quests.explanation: The paragraph sets early access against certainty and shows that regulators, patients and safety advocates weigh them differently. The wrong options reverse the risk of shortened trials, the reliability of follow-up and patient groups' view.
keyPoints: Regulators must decide how quickly to approve medicines.
Faster approval helps patients but may miss rare side effects, and conditional approval relies on follow-up.
Patient groups and safety advocates differ on how much risk is acceptable.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Speakers of regional dialects are sometimes judged less intelligent or less professional than speakers of the standard form. Research shows that these judgements affect hiring and grades, even when the content of what is said is identical. Some parents encourage children to modify their accent to avoid disadvantage. Linguists stress that all dialects are equally complex and rule-governed, and that the prestige of the standard language is a matter of history and power. Employers and schools have begun training staff to recognise accent bias. Critics reply that people still need mastery of the standard form to access certain opportunities. Many sociolinguists therefore advocate being able to switch between forms. They argue that the burden of adjusting should not always fall on the speaker.
options: Accent bias disadvantages dialect speakers so both flexible speakers and fairer institutions are needed.
Sociolinguists argue that dialect speakers alone should adjust, since institutions cannot change their attitudes.
Linguists say that standard languages are more complex than regional dialects, so the bias is justified.
Research shows accent has little effect on hiring or grades when what people say is identical.
quests.correctAnswer: Accent bias disadvantages dialect speakers so both flexible speakers and fairer institutions are needed.
quests.hint: Notice who the final sentence says should share the effort of change.
quests.explanation: The paragraph documents bias, challenges its basis and recommends flexibility on both sides, not only from the speaker. The wrong options reverse linguists' claim, the research finding and the sociolinguists' view.
keyPoints: People who speak regional dialects are often judged less capable.
Linguists say all dialects are equally complex, and the standard's prestige is historical.
Speakers may need to switch forms, but institutions should also address bias.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Colonial-era archives contain records that could help families trace their history and help historians study the past. Many of these documents were taken to the former colonial power, so people in the countries they describe cannot easily consult them. Digitisation offers a partial answer, but it requires funds that poorer institutions lack. Some archives worry about sharing records that name individuals, since descendants may be affected. Others hold that secrecy simply protects those who committed abuses. Several countries have begun to return original documents or to share copies under joint management. Historians caution that the transfer of files does not by itself ensure that the stories they contain will be told. Access, they say, is the beginning of a much longer process.
options: Digitisation of colonial archives is cheap, so poorer institutions can readily provide access to records.
Archives agree that secrecy is needed because sharing records would not help descendants or historians.
Sharing colonial archives widens access to history, but privacy, funding and interpretation remain difficult even after files move.
Historians say that returning documents ensures that the stories they contain will be told.
quests.correctAnswer: Sharing colonial archives widens access to history, but privacy, funding and interpretation remain difficult even after files move.
quests.hint: Check which option respects the writer's warning in the last two sentences.
quests.explanation: The paragraph outlines a legitimate need for access, complications and partial solutions, and closes by warning that access is only a start. The wrong options claim digitisation is cheap, invent agreement on secrecy and claim transfer ensures interpretation.
keyPoints: Colonial records are held far from the people they describe.
Digitisation and returns help, but funding and privacy concerns remain.
Historians say access begins a longer process of interpretation.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A hospital introduced software that predicts which emergency patients are most likely to deteriorate. Doctors found that it caught some cases they would have missed. But an audit showed that the software gave lower risk scores to patients from poorer areas, because it had been trained on past data in which those patients received less care. Staff who trusted the score without question therefore risked repeating existing inequalities. The developers retrained the model and introduced regular checks by group. Clinicians were also reminded that the score is advice, not a verdict. The hospital now reports that the tool helps most when doctors combine it with their own judgement. Its designers emphasise that no dataset is neutral.
options: The software gave higher risk scores to poorer patients, which made doctors reduce their care.
The audit showed the software was neutral because it had been trained on a complete and fair dataset.
Predictive software can inherit past inequalities so it needs checking and human judgement.
Doctors found that the software caught few cases they would have missed, so it was discontinued.
quests.correctAnswer: Predictive software can inherit past inequalities so it needs checking and human judgement.
quests.hint: Ask why the software's flaw was invisible until someone checked, and what that implies for its use.
quests.explanation: The tool was useful but reproduced unequal patterns, so retraining, monitoring and human oversight are needed. The wrong options reverse the direction of bias, the software's usefulness and the neutrality of data.
keyPoints: Software predicted which emergency patients might deteriorate and caught missed cases.
An audit found it gave lower scores to poorer patients, reflecting past unequal care.
Retraining, checks and clinical judgement make the tool safer.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Seed vaults store copies of crop varieties to protect them from disasters and loss. Most vaults hold seeds that were collected decades ago, and they are frozen, so they do not adapt to changing conditions. Farmers who continue to grow traditional varieties in their fields keep them evolving in response to pests and weather. Some conservationists therefore argue that living farms are a better insurance than freezers. Yet a vault is safe from wars, floods and shifts in farming fashions, and it can restore varieties that have vanished from fields. Advocates suggest that the two approaches work best together, with vault seeds returned to farmers regularly. Funding, however, tends to favour the more visible and easier vault. The result is an imbalance between preservation and use.
options: Vaults and farm-grown varieties protect crop diversity in different ways and funding favours frozen storage.
Vault seeds continue evolving in response to pests and weather because they are stored frozen.
Conservationists agree that vaults alone are sufficient, since farms cannot protect traditional varieties.
Funding favours living farms over vaults, because farms are more visible and cheaper to support.
quests.correctAnswer: Vaults and farm-grown varieties protect crop diversity in different ways and funding favours frozen storage.
quests.hint: See how the paragraph gives each method a strength and a weakness before making its final point.
quests.explanation: Each approach has advantages, complementarity is proposed and funding is skewed toward the vault. The wrong options reverse how frozen seeds behave, conservationists' view and the direction of the funding imbalance.
keyPoints: Seed vaults freeze old varieties, so the seeds cannot adapt.
Farm-grown varieties evolve, but vaults survive disasters and restore lost types.
The two work best together, but funding favours vaults.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: When airlines merge, passengers often see fewer routes and higher fares on the routes where competition disappears. Airlines argue that consolidation lets them survive in an industry with thin profits and heavy fuel costs. Regulators sometimes approve mergers only if the companies give up landing slots at busy airports so that rivals can enter. This can restore competition on paper, but new entrants may lack the resources to use the slots well. Economists find mixed results: some mergers lower costs and improve service, while others simply raise prices. Consumer groups say that regulators should judge mergers by their effect on passengers, not on airline finances. The outcome often depends on how easy it is for newcomers to gain a foothold.
options: Airline mergers lower fares because consolidation reduces costs and strengthens competition on routes.
Regulators approve mergers when companies keep their landing slots at busy airports.
Consumer groups say regulators should judge mergers mainly by their effect on airline finances.
Airline mergers can help or harm passengers depending on whether newcomers can enter routes.
quests.correctAnswer: Airline mergers can help or harm passengers depending on whether newcomers can enter routes.
quests.hint: Find the sentence that explains what determines whether a merger helps or harms passengers.
quests.explanation: Results vary, and effective entry by rivals is what decides whether competition is preserved. The wrong options overgeneralise the benefit, reverse the slot condition and reverse the consumer groups' criterion.
keyPoints: Mergers can reduce routes and raise fares where competition disappears.
Regulators may require slot releases, but newcomers may struggle to use them.
Economists find mixed results, depending on entry.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Some countries impose mandatory minimum prison sentences for certain crimes. Supporters argue that they ensure consistency and deter offenders. Judges complain that the rules prevent them from considering the circumstances of the case, so that a first-time offender may receive the same term as a hardened criminal. Studies find little evidence that longer mandatory terms deter crime more than the likelihood of being caught. They also increase prison populations and costs. Prosecutors sometimes respond by charging suspects with lesser offences to avoid the minimum, which shifts power from judges to prosecutors. Reformers therefore suggest guidelines that leave judges some discretion but require them to explain departures. The debate concerns who should hold the power to decide fairness.
options: Studies show that longer mandatory terms deter crime more effectively than a greater chance of being caught.
Prosecutors are unaffected by minimum sentences because charging decisions do not change the punishment offenders receive.
Judges support mandatory minimums because the rules let them consider each offender's circumstances.
Mandatory minimums promise consistency and shift discretion to prosecutors so guided judicial discretion is proposed.
quests.correctAnswer: Mandatory minimums promise consistency and shift discretion to prosecutors so guided judicial discretion is proposed.
quests.hint: Follow how a rule meant to limit one group's power increases another's.
quests.explanation: Minimums limit judges but encourage plea and charging strategies that move discretion elsewhere, so reformers propose guidelines. The wrong options reverse deterrence evidence, judges' view and the effect on prosecutors.
keyPoints: Mandatory minimum sentences aim at consistency and deterrence.
Judges lose discretion, prosecutors gain influence, and evidence of extra deterrence is weak.
Reformers suggest guidelines that require judges to explain departures.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: In several African countries, children begin school in a language they do not speak at home, such as English or French. Teachers may themselves be less than fluent, so lessons rely on memorising rather than understanding. Research shows that children learn to read faster when they begin in the language they know. Yet parents often prefer the international language, seeing it as the key to jobs and further study. Textbooks in local languages are scarce and costly to produce. Some programmes teach in the home language for several years, then introduce the international language as a subject. Results are encouraging where teachers are trained and books are supplied. Otherwise, good intentions fail for lack of materials.
options: Parents prefer home-language instruction because they see it as the key to further study.
Learning first in a familiar language works, but parents' preferences and shortages limit it.
Textbooks in local languages are plentiful and inexpensive, so materials are not a problem.
Children learn to read faster in an unfamiliar international language because it is used for jobs.
quests.correctAnswer: Learning first in a familiar language works, but parents' preferences and shortages limit it.
quests.hint: Distinguish what research recommends from what parents want and what schools can actually supply.
quests.explanation: Research favours home-language starts, parents may prefer international languages and resources are a constraint. The wrong options reverse the reading finding, textbook availability and parents' preference.
keyPoints: Many children begin school in a language they do not speak at home.
Reading improves when they start in a familiar language, but parents often prefer the international one.
Programmes succeed only where teachers are trained and books supplied.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Countries with strict climate rules worry that their factories will lose business to competitors in countries with weaker rules. A carbon border tax would charge importers for the emissions embedded in goods such as steel and cement. Supporters say this protects domestic industry and encourages other countries to cut emissions. Critics say that it could be seen as disguised protectionism, and that it burdens poorer exporters who lack the money to clean up their industries. Measuring embedded emissions is also technically difficult and easy to dispute. Some proposals return the revenue to affected developing countries, to soften the impact. Whether the measure will speed global action or trigger trade disputes is unclear. Much depends on how other governments respond.
options: A carbon border tax aims to prevent industry flight and risks disputes and burdens poorer exporters.
The tax has ended trade disputes by persuading governments to accept the same emission rules.
Critics say the tax is easy to measure and benefits poorer exporters who cannot clean up.
A carbon border tax would charge exporters, not importers, for emissions embedded in steel and cement.
quests.correctAnswer: A carbon border tax aims to prevent industry flight and risks disputes and burdens poorer exporters.
quests.hint: Give the aim, the objections and the words that show the outcome is still open.
quests.explanation: The measure addresses a competitive worry but faces fairness, measurement and diplomatic problems, and its effect is uncertain. The wrong options reverse who pays, the critics' claim and the current outcome.
keyPoints: Strict climate rules make some countries fear losing industry to weaker rivals.
A border tax would charge importers for embedded emissions, but critics see protectionism and burden.
Measurement is hard, and whether it speeds action or triggers disputes is unclear.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Academic tenure protects professors from being dismissed for unpopular research or opinions. Supporters say that it allows scholars to pursue difficult questions without fear of pressure from funders or politicians. Critics argue that it can shelter unproductive staff and that universities increasingly rely on temporary contracts for teaching, which weakens the protection for the majority. Younger researchers may spend a decade on short contracts before a permanent post becomes available. Some institutions offer long-term contracts with periodic review, which provide security without absolute permanence. Academics worry that these arrangements will not protect controversial work. Administrators reply that unfair dismissals are rare. The question is whether academic freedom can survive without strong job security.
options: Tenure now protects most university teachers, because temporary contracts are used for research.
Tenure protects academic freedom, and temporary contracts leave most scholars unprotected.
Younger researchers usually receive permanent posts within a year, so temporary contracts are not a concern.
Administrators claim that unfair dismissals are common, so long-term contracts cannot protect anyone.
quests.correctAnswer: Tenure protects academic freedom, and temporary contracts leave most scholars unprotected.
quests.hint: Watch for an option that talks only about the professors who already have tenure.
quests.explanation: Tenure is defended as freedom's guard, yet most teaching staff lack it, and alternatives are contested. The wrong options reverse how many are protected, administrators' claim and the wait for permanent posts.
keyPoints: Tenure shields professors from dismissal over unpopular work.
Many teaching staff are on temporary contracts, and young researchers wait long for permanent posts.
Long-term contracts offer partial security, but academics doubt they protect controversial work.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Banks are required to pass stress tests that simulate a severe recession, so that regulators can check whether they would survive heavy losses. The tests have made banks hold more capital, and the system was more resilient during recent shocks. However, banks can prepare for known scenarios, and the tests may miss threats that nobody has imagined. Critics also worry that if all banks respond to the same test in the same way, they may all sell the same assets when trouble comes. Regulators are therefore adding surprise scenarios and looking at links between banks and non-bank lenders. Some experts propose that publishing results helps market discipline. Others fear that it could trigger panic. Stress tests reduce risk without eliminating it.
options: Banks that pass the tests behave differently from one another, which prevents shared selling in a crisis.
Experts agree that publishing results improves market discipline and does not cause panic.
Stress tests have reduced the risk of banking crises, so regulators keep adding surprise scenarios.
Stress tests strengthen bank resilience but reduce risk without removing it.
quests.correctAnswer: Stress tests strengthen bank resilience but reduce risk without removing it.
quests.hint: Pay attention to the closing sentence, which is more modest than the opening claims of the tests.
quests.explanation: The tests bring real improvements but have blind spots that regulators try to close, and they cannot remove all risk. The wrong options claim elimination, reverse herd behaviour and overstate experts' agreement.
keyPoints: Stress tests simulate severe recessions and have led banks to hold more capital.
Banks can prepare for known scenarios, and similar responses may cause herd selling.
Regulators add surprise scenarios, but risk is reduced rather than eliminated.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: For decades, forest managers put out every fire quickly, and undergrowth built up over the years. When a fire finally takes hold, it burns hotter and spreads faster than the ones that once cleared the forest floor gently. Some managers now light small, controlled fires in cooler seasons to remove fuel. Indigenous peoples practised similar burning for centuries, and their knowledge is being sought again. Prescribed burning carries risks, since a fire can escape or send smoke into towns. Managers must wait for the right weather and have enough crews, which limits how much land can be treated. Even so, studies show that treated areas suffer less severe damage when wildfires arrive. The old policy of suppression, it seems, created the problem it aimed to prevent.
options: Prescribed burning is easy to carry out throughout the year because crews are available.
Indigenous peoples avoided burning forests, so their knowledge is irrelevant to modern fire managers.
Suppressing every fire let fuel build up, so controlled burning is being revived with its limits.
Controlled burning is unnecessary because forests that suppress fires burn gently when fires arrive.
quests.correctAnswer: Suppressing every fire let fuel build up, so controlled burning is being revived with its limits.
quests.hint: Notice the irony in the last sentence and choose the option that captures it.
quests.explanation: Past suppression produced conditions for severe fires, and controlled burns are a partial remedy with practical limits. The wrong options reverse fire intensity, Indigenous practice and the ease of burning.
keyPoints: Decades of fire suppression let undergrowth accumulate.
Managers now use small controlled burns, drawing on Indigenous knowledge.
Risks and weather limits restrict burning, but treated areas suffer less damage.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Thousands of new satellites are being launched to provide internet access to remote areas. For villages without cables or towers, this could be transformative. Astronomers, however, complain that satellites leave bright streaks across telescope images and disrupt observations of faint objects. Companies have darkened their satellites and adjusted their positions, which has reduced the problem but not solved it. Some scientists worry that as numbers grow into the tens of thousands, the night sky will change for everyone. Others point out that satellites can also help science by providing data links and monitoring the atmosphere. There are no clear international rules about how much interference is acceptable. The conflict shows how new infrastructure can create costs for those who never chose to bear them.
options: Satellite internet offers connectivity and harms astronomy and no clear rule limits interference.
International rules already set clear limits on how much interference satellites are permitted to cause.
Astronomers say satellites cause little interference because satellites are too faint to appear in telescope images.
Satellite streaks have been eliminated because companies have darkened their satellites and moved their positions.
quests.correctAnswer: Satellite internet offers connectivity and harms astronomy and no clear rule limits interference.
quests.hint: Note who benefits, who pays the cost and whether a rule exists to arbitrate.
quests.explanation: The benefit to remote users is set against the costs to observers, mitigation is partial and governance is lacking. The wrong options claim the problem is solved, deny interference and claim rules exist.
keyPoints: New satellites could bring internet to remote areas.
Astronomers report streaks in images, which darkening reduces but does not remove.
There are no clear international rules on acceptable interference.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Large charitable foundations hold assets worth billions and can fund projects that governments and markets ignore. Their independence allows them to take risks and to support unpopular causes. Yet they are not elected, and their priorities reflect the views of their founders. Critics question whether wealthy donors should shape public policy, from schools to health, without public debate. Foundations have sometimes funded promising ideas, then withdrawn support before the work was secure. Grantees complain that complex reporting demands consume time. Some foundations have begun to publish their strategies openly and to consult the communities they serve. They argue that humility about what they know is essential to doing good. Transparency, they add, is the price of influence.
options: Grantees say reporting demands are minimal, and that foundations rarely withdraw support from projects.
Foundations argue that transparency is unnecessary because their independence already protects them from criticism.
Foundations are elected bodies whose priorities reflect the views of the communities they serve.
Foundations can fund neglected causes, and their unaccountable influence prompts calls for transparency and consultation.
quests.correctAnswer: Foundations can fund neglected causes, and their unaccountable influence prompts calls for transparency and consultation.
quests.hint: Identify what the paragraph says the foundations must give in return for their influence.
quests.explanation: Independence enables valuable risk-taking but confers unaccountable influence, and openness is presented as the price of that influence. The wrong options reverse election, grantees' experience and foundations' position.
keyPoints: Foundations can fund neglected projects and take risks.
They are unelected, and critics question their influence and sudden withdrawals.
Some now publish strategies and consult communities, accepting transparency.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: School voucher schemes give parents public money to spend at the school of their choice, including private schools. Supporters say that competition will push all schools to improve and that poor families should have the same options as rich ones. Critics reply that the best schools may select their pupils, leaving weaker schools with the hardest cases and less money. Evidence is mixed: some studies find modest gains for students who use vouchers, while others find none. Effects on the wider system are harder to measure. Transport and information are barriers, since families need to know their options and how to reach them. Design details such as admissions rules and accountability therefore matter greatly. The idea works or fails according to how it is built.
options: Supporters argue that competition weakens schools, so poor families need fewer options than rich ones.
Vouchers may widen choice and results depend on design details such as admissions, information and accountability.
Critics say the best schools are open to pupils, so weaker schools do not lose money.
Vouchers have produced large gains for students who used them, according to studies.
quests.correctAnswer: Vouchers may widen choice and results depend on design details such as admissions, information and accountability.
quests.hint: Decide whether the paragraph treats vouchers as good, bad or dependent on something else.
quests.explanation: The evidence is mixed, and the effect depends on rules and practical barriers, as the last sentence says. The wrong options claim consistent gains, reverse the selection concern and reverse the supporters' argument.
keyPoints: Vouchers let parents use public money at any school, including private ones.
Supporters cite competition and equal options, while critics fear selection and weaker schools.
Evidence is mixed, so admissions rules, information and accountability matter.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Governments keep stockpiles of medicines, masks and equipment in case of a pandemic. Stockpiles can be a lifeline, but they cost money to store and expire if they are not used. In the years between emergencies, budgets are tight and stocks may be allowed to run down. Some countries rotate supplies through normal hospital use to keep them fresh. Others contract with manufacturers to make more quickly when needed, which saves storage costs but depends on the factories being ready. Experts add that supplies are useless without trained staff and clear plans to distribute them. During the last crisis, several countries found shelves empty or full of unusable equipment. Preparedness, they conclude, is a habit, not a purchase.
options: Stockpiles keep indefinitely, so governments can safely leave supplies untouched between emergencies.
Stockpiles help only when maintained, rotated and backed by trained staff and plans.
During the last crisis, countries found their shelves full of usable equipment ready for distribution.
Contracts with manufacturers remove the need for planning or trained staff during a crisis.
quests.correctAnswer: Stockpiles help only when maintained, rotated and backed by trained staff and plans.
quests.hint: Look at the closing remark. It compresses the message of the whole paragraph.
quests.explanation: Stocks decay without attention and must be paired with trained people and plans, so preparedness is continuous effort. The wrong options claim supplies never expire, remove planning and reverse the crisis experience.
keyPoints: Governments hold medicines, masks and equipment for pandemics.
Stocks expire or run down when budgets are tight.
Rotation, contracts, training and distribution plans are needed, as preparedness is a habit.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Museums that hold objects taken during conflict or colonial rule face growing demands to return them. Some have agreed, arguing that it is the right thing to do. Others fear that returning objects will set a precedent that could empty their collections. Legal arguments are complicated, because laws in force when objects were acquired may differ from present standards. Source communities also ask that objects be displayed with their own explanations. Countries requesting returns must also show that they can care for the objects. In some cases, museums and source communities have agreed on shared custody or long-term loans. Curators say that the process often builds relationships that support research and exhibitions. It seems that the most durable solutions arise from negotiation, not from confrontation in courtrooms.
options: Curators say returns end relationships between museums and source communities and damage exhibitions.
Legal arguments over restitution are simple, because acquisition laws matched present standards in most cases.
Museums have agreed to return the objects taken during conflict or colonial rule.
Restitution disputes are increasingly settled through negotiated arrangements such as loans and shared custody.
quests.correctAnswer: Restitution disputes are increasingly settled through negotiated arrangements such as loans and shared custody.
quests.hint: Find the sentence that generalises about what works best and check the option against it.
quests.explanation: The paragraph presents disagreement and legal complexity, then points to negotiated arrangements as the most durable. The wrong options reverse legal clarity, museums' agreement and curators' experience.
keyPoints: Museums face demands to return objects taken in conflict or colonial rule.
Some agree to return them, others fear precedent, and law is complicated.
Loans and shared custody built through negotiation seem most durable.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Wind and solar power vary with weather, so grids need ways to store energy for calm, dark periods. Batteries can cover a few hours, and their cost has fallen dramatically. But storing energy for days or weeks is more challenging. Long-duration options are still early in development and expensive to build. Options include pumping water uphill, making hydrogen and using surplus power to heat materials that release heat later. Each has a different balance of cost, efficiency and location requirements. Grid operators also point out that connecting distant regions reduces the need for storage, since weather differs from place to place. Building the connections requires long planning and public acceptance. The cheapest system will probably combine storage of several kinds with better transmission and flexible demand.
options: Hydrogen is the cheapest storage method in most locations, so grid operators should rely on it.
Connecting distant regions increases the need for storage because weather is similar across regions.
Renewable grids will probably combine several storage kinds with connections and flexible demand.
Batteries can already store energy for weeks, so other storage options are unnecessary for grids.
quests.correctAnswer: Renewable grids will probably combine several storage kinds with connections and flexible demand.
quests.hint: Watch for options that promote one storage technology when the paragraph advocates a mixture.
quests.explanation: Different storage timescales require different technologies, and connections and flexible demand reduce the need, so a mix is likely. The wrong options overstate batteries, reverse the effect of connections and single out hydrogen.
keyPoints: Renewable power varies, so grids need storage.
Batteries handle hours, but longer storage uses water, hydrogen or heat.
Connections and flexible demand reduce storage needs, so a mixed system is likely.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Farmers face risks from droughts, floods and price swings, and insurance can help them recover after a bad year. In poorer countries, traditional insurance is expensive to run because assessing individual losses is costly. Index insurance pays out when rainfall falls below a set level, without visiting farms. This lowers costs and speeds up payments. But if a farmer's own field suffers although the rainfall measure looks normal, no payment is made, which can breed distrust. Studies show that farmers with insurance are willing to invest more in seed and fertiliser, since they are protected from disaster. Governments often subsidise premiums to make the product affordable. Trust, more than price, tends to decide whether farmers buy it.
options: Price is the main factor that determines whether farmers buy index insurance, according to the paragraph.
Index insurance requires assessors to visit each farm, which is why payouts are quick and cheap.
Farmers with insurance invest less in seed and fertiliser because they feel protected from disaster.
Index insurance is cheap and fast and mismatches between the index and losses limit trust.
quests.correctAnswer: Index insurance is cheap and fast and mismatches between the index and losses limit trust.
quests.hint: Choose the option that keeps the benefit alongside the weakness that the last sentence highlights.
quests.explanation: Index insurance lowers cost and speeds payment and encourages investment, but it can miss individual losses, so trust decides uptake. The wrong options reverse how payouts are made, the effect on investment and the role of price.
keyPoints: Insurance helps farmers recover from droughts, floods and price swings.
Index insurance pays when rainfall falls below a set level, lowering cost and delay.
Mismatches between the index and real losses can damage trust.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Health researchers often share datasets after removing names and addresses. Yet studies show that people can sometimes be identified by combining such data with other information, such as birth date, postcode and sex. As more information becomes public, the risk of re-identification grows. Some researchers now add small amounts of random noise to their data, which protects individuals but reduces accuracy. Others keep the data in secure environments where researchers can run analyses without downloading it. Patients often say that they are happy for their data to help research, provided they are protected from misuse. Regulators have begun to require formal risk assessments before health data is shared. The challenge is balancing the value of open data against the duty to protect participants. No approach removes the trade-off entirely.
options: Removing names does not guarantee anonymity, so researchers must balance data usefulness against privacy.
Adding random noise protects individuals and also improves the accuracy of health research findings.
Removing names and addresses makes re-identification impossible, so open sharing carries little privacy risk.
Patients refuse to share their data, so researchers have abandoned secure environments for public datasets.
quests.correctAnswer: Removing names does not guarantee anonymity, so researchers must balance data usefulness against privacy.
quests.hint: Compare what each protective method gains with what it costs.
quests.explanation: Anonymised data can still identify people, and each protective method sacrifices some utility or convenience, so the trade-off remains. The wrong options claim guaranteed anonymity, reverse the effect of noise and misstate patients' attitudes.
keyPoints: Datasets shared without names can still identify people through other information.
Random noise and secure environments protect privacy but cost accuracy or convenience.
Patients accept research use if protected, but the trade-off cannot be removed.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Economies are shifting from manufacturing towards services such as healthcare, education and finance. Services provide many jobs, but productivity in them grows more slowly, because a haircut or a lesson cannot be speeded up as easily as a car assembly line. As a result, wages in some service sectors have stagnated while prices, particularly for education and healthcare, keep rising. Some economists call this cost disease and worry that governments will find these services ever harder to afford. Others reply that technology is beginning to change services too, through online delivery and automation. Some governments have responded by raising public spending on services faster than overall growth. Yet quality often depends on human attention, which technology may not replace. The question is how to maintain and pay for essential services in economies where the human element is the product.
options: Economists agree that technology has already made human attention unnecessary in healthcare and education.
Service productivity grows faster than manufacturing productivity, so prices for education and healthcare are falling.
Slow productivity growth raises service costs, leaving societies to decide how to afford them.
Wages in service sectors have risen sharply as prices have stayed level in education and healthcare.
quests.correctAnswer: Slow productivity growth raises service costs, leaving societies to decide how to afford them.
quests.hint: Identify the cause of rising costs and the limits of technology as an answer.
quests.explanation: Services resist productivity gains, so their costs rise faster, and technology may not fully substitute human attention. The wrong options reverse productivity, economists' agreement and the wage and price pattern.
keyPoints: Economies are shifting toward services like healthcare and education.
Productivity in services grows slowly, so costs rise while wages stagnate.
Technology may help partly, but the human element is central.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Vaccine patents give companies exclusive rights to manufacture their products for many years. Supporters say the rights reward the huge cost and risk of development. During the pandemic, many governments argued that temporary waivers would allow more factories to make vaccines and shorten shortages. Opponents replied that the main obstacles were not legal but practical, such as scarce ingredients and the skills needed to make the vaccines safely. Voluntary licensing agreements and technology-sharing hubs were arranged as alternatives. Health advocates said these arrangements were too slow and too limited. Companies pointed to the speed with which the vaccines had been developed as evidence that incentives work. The disagreement shows that ownership rules and manufacturing capacity are separate problems.
options: Debates over vaccine patents show that ownership rules and manufacturing capacity are separate obstacles.
Voluntary licensing agreements were praised by health advocates as faster and broader than a waiver.
Opponents argued that patents were the main obstacle, since ingredients and skills were plentiful.
Companies said the speed of development showed that incentives were unnecessary for producing vaccines.
quests.correctAnswer: Debates over vaccine patents show that ownership rules and manufacturing capacity are separate obstacles.
quests.hint: Ask what the last sentence claims that the two sides had been mixing up.
quests.explanation: The debate over waivers versus incentives obscured that lifting patents does not automatically create factories or ingredients. The wrong options reverse the opponents' argument, advocates' view and companies' reasoning.
keyPoints: Patents reward development, but governments proposed waivers to widen production.
Opponents said scarce ingredients and skills were the real obstacles.
Licensing hubs were arranged, and the dispute shows legal and practical problems differ.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Cities that run buses, trams and trains under separate operators often have separate fares and tickets. Passengers who change between services may pay several times for one journey. Integrated fares, in which a single ticket works across operators and caps the daily total, make trips simpler and cheaper for people who change vehicles. Ridership tends to rise, and the change helps those who cannot afford expensive single fares. But operators worry about losing revenue and about how to share the income fairly. Setting up the systems requires agreement between authorities that may have competing interests. Passengers in trial cities also reported feeling less anxious about choosing routes. Cities that succeeded usually created a single body to plan services and set fares. Convenience, it appears, requires coordination.
options: Integrated fares reduce ridership because passengers who change vehicles pay more for their journeys.
Cities succeeded by keeping separate authorities so that each operator could set its own fares.
Integrated fares make journeys simpler and cheaper and require coordination and fair revenue sharing.
Operators welcome integrated fares because they guarantee higher revenue for each separate operator.
quests.correctAnswer: Integrated fares make journeys simpler and cheaper and require coordination and fair revenue sharing.
quests.hint: Find the condition that the last sentence attaches to convenience.
quests.explanation: A single ticket benefits passengers but requires operators and authorities to coordinate and share revenue. The wrong options reverse the ridership effect, operators' attitude and the cities' structure.
keyPoints: Separate operators can make passengers pay repeatedly for one journey.
Integrated fares with caps simplify travel and raise ridership.
Revenue sharing and coordination are challenges, and a single planning body helps.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Labels such as sustainable seafood help consumers to choose fish caught in ways that protect stocks. Independent auditors check fisheries against standards, and supermarkets often promise to sell only certified fish. Studies find that certified fisheries have somewhat healthier stocks and fewer accidental catches. Yet critics observe that many fisheries were already well managed before certification, so the label may reward rather than reform. Small-scale fishers in poorer countries often cannot afford the fees for auditing. As a result, most certified fish comes from large operations in wealthy regions. Consumers, meanwhile, rarely check what a label actually requires of a fishery. Some programmes have added discounts or group certification to help small fishers. Labels are a useful tool, but they do not by themselves solve overfishing.
options: Certified fisheries were mostly poorly managed before certification, so the label clearly transforms fishing.
Seafood labels reward sustainable fishing but exclude small fishers and cannot solve overfishing alone.
Small-scale fishers in poorer countries can readily afford auditing fees, which supermarkets subsidise.
Most certified fish comes from small operations in poorer regions, because their standards are highest.
quests.correctAnswer: Seafood labels reward sustainable fishing but exclude small fishers and cannot solve overfishing alone.
quests.hint: Check whether an option makes the label sound like a complete cure.
quests.explanation: Certification has positive but limited effects, rewarding those who were already doing well and excluding others. The wrong options reverse the earlier management, small fishers' costs and the source of certified fish.
keyPoints: Sustainability labels guide consumers toward better-managed fisheries.
Certified fisheries show healthier stocks, but many were already well run.
Fees exclude small-scale fishers, so labels alone cannot solve overfishing.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Millions of refugee children are out of school, sometimes for years. Host countries may lack classroom space, and refugee families may not have the documents needed to enrol. Some countries have opened their schools to refugees, using double shifts so that local and refugee children can share buildings. Teachers often need training to support children who have experienced trauma and who speak a different language. Funding is a chronic problem, since aid for education is small compared with aid for food and shelter. Yet education gives children stability and hope, and it prepares them for return or resettlement. Researchers say that including refugees in national systems is more effective than running separate camps schools. It also avoids creating a lost generation.
options: Aid for education is larger than aid for food and shelter, so funding is rarely a problem.
Refugee children usually enrol without documents, so host countries face few barriers to inclusion.
Including refugee children in national schools works, and space, training and funding are obstacles.
Separate camp schools are more effective than national systems, according to researchers.
quests.correctAnswer: Including refugee children in national schools works, and space, training and funding are obstacles.
quests.hint: Consider the practical barriers and the reason researchers still favour inclusion.
quests.explanation: The paragraph describes barriers and a preferred solution supported by research and by its long-term benefits. The wrong options reverse funding levels, researchers' preference and documentation problems.
keyPoints: Many refugee children miss school for years because of space and documents.
Double shifts help, but teachers need training and funding is low.
Researchers favour national inclusion because it provides stability and avoids a lost generation.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Companies have been pressed to increase the diversity of their boards, and many now set targets for the number of women or minority directors. Research suggests that diverse boards discuss a wider range of ideas and may catch risks that a uniform group overlooks. Yet studies of financial results are inconsistent, and some show no effect. Critics also argue that targets can encourage token appointments that leave power unchanged. Supporters answer that without targets, progress is very slow and that a fair board is justified in itself, whatever the profits. Some firms have gone further by widening the pool of candidates and offering mentoring to those from under-represented groups. Investors are increasingly asking companies to report on how directors are chosen. Real change, they say, depends on culture, not counting.
options: Supporters say that targets are unnecessary because progress would be quick without them.
Critics claim that targets give under-represented directors more power than other board members.
Studies consistently show that diverse boards raise financial results, so diversity targets are profitable.
Board diversity may improve discussion, but targets alone may not change real influence.
quests.correctAnswer: Board diversity may improve discussion, but targets alone may not change real influence.
quests.hint: See how the final sentence moves the argument from numbers to something less easy to measure.
quests.explanation: Diversity has arguable benefits, but targets are contested and the paragraph concludes that culture matters most. The wrong options claim consistent results, reverse supporters' stance and reverse critics' worry.
keyPoints: Companies set targets to diversify their boards.
Diverse boards may discuss more ideas, but financial evidence is mixed and tokenism is feared.
Widening candidate pools and mentoring aim at real cultural change.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Within some unions of countries, citizens are free to live and work in any member state. Workers gain opportunities, and employers can fill vacancies. But the movement is uneven, and some regions lose young, skilled people who might have contributed to their local economies. Sending countries receive money from workers abroad, which supports families but does not replace the loss of nurses and engineers. Receiving regions benefit from workers but may see pressure on housing and services. Studies find that the overall economic effect is positive, though the gains and losses are spread unevenly. Policymakers therefore use funds to support regions that lose people and to help those that receive them. Free movement is an economic tool that produces social consequences.
options: Studies show that free movement harms the economy overall, though gains are spread evenly.
Free movement brings overall gains and uneven local effects so funds support affected regions.
Receiving regions face little pressure on housing or services, so they need little support from funds.
Sending regions gain most from free movement because remittances make up for the loss of skilled workers.
quests.correctAnswer: Free movement brings overall gains and uneven local effects so funds support affected regions.
quests.hint: Look for how the paragraph distinguishes overall benefit from local impact.
quests.explanation: The overall effect is positive but distribution matters, which explains policies to support affected regions. The wrong options reverse the effect of remittances, the overall finding and the receiving regions' experience.
keyPoints: Citizens of some unions can live and work in any member state.
Overall effects are positive, but sending regions lose skilled people and receiving regions face pressure.
Funds are used to help both kinds of region.
